landing.intro: Twelve interactive simulators for the design, operation, maintenance and energy management of lifts and escalators.

sim1.title: Traffic Flow Simulator
sim1.short: Visualise peak passenger flow; compute handling capacity and waiting time.
sim1.standard: CIBSE Guide D (2020); Barney up-peak RTT
sim1.insight: With {{cars}} lifts of {{cap}} persons at {{speed}} m/s, the round-trip time is about {{rtt}} s, giving an interval of {{int}} s and a 5-minute handling capacity of {{hc}}%. Average up-peak waiting time is roughly {{awt}} s. A shorter interval (more/faster/bigger cars) means shorter waits; handling capacity must exceed the building's peak arrival rate (typically 11–15% of population for offices).
sim1.awtMeaning: Why the wait isn't simply half the interval: average waiting time is a fraction of the interval set by the traffic pattern, not a fixed half. For {{profile}} that fraction is {{factor}}, so AWT ≈ {{factor}} × {{int}} s ≈ {{awt}} s. The half-interval rule only holds when passengers arrive at random and lifts arrive at perfectly even gaps. In practice lifts bunch (uneven gaps), and in a down-peak they fill at upper floors and bypass lower landings — both make people wait longer. So the fraction climbs from 0.40 (up-peak: cars leave the lobby in turn, keeping gaps even) through 0.50 (inter-floor) and 0.55 (two-way) to 0.60 (down-peak: the most irregular). In this teaching model the traffic profile changes only this waiting-time fraction — the round-trip time, interval and handling capacity stay fixed by the up-peak sizing method.
sim1.notes: Use with Module 2. Interval and handling capacity are the two headline metrics. Rule of thumb: office up-peak target HC ≈ 11–15% and INT ≤ 30 s. Watch how adding a car, raising speed or increasing capacity changes RTT and INT. Note: served population = population/floor × floors (see DECISIONS T1 on the brief's 12–14% band).

sim2.title: Group Control Comparison
sim2.short: Conventional vs destination control — stops and waiting time.
sim2.insight: Over {{runs}} simulated up-peak runs, destination control groups passengers by floor so each car makes {{dcsStops}} stops per trip versus {{collStops}} for collective control — {{stopRed}}% fewer stops. That shortens the round trip and cuts average waiting time by {{awtRed}}% ({{collAwt}} s → {{dcsAwt}} s). Fewer stops also means lower energy per trip.
sim2.notes: Use with Module 2. DCS asks passengers for their destination at the lobby and batches those going to the same floors into one car — so cars make far fewer stops. The split view runs the same random passenger stream through both algorithms. Expect ≥20% lower waiting and ≥25% fewer stops. Trade-off: passengers must enter their floor before boarding (a behaviour change).

sim3.title: Lift Sizing Wizard
sim3.short: Recommend a lift configuration from a building brief.
sim3.noResults: No configuration meets the target. Lower the handling-capacity target or reduce occupants.
sim3.insight: For {{occupants}} occupants over {{floors}} floors, the recommended configuration is {{cars}} cars of {{load}} kg at {{speed}} m/s, with a {{drive}} machine and {{group}} group control — interval {{int}} s, handling capacity {{hc}}%. Fewer, well-sized shafts beat many small cars: each shaft consumes valuable building core area.
sim3.notes: Use with Module 2. The wizard searches car-count × capacity × speed combinations and ranks the feasible ones. Key teaching point: minimise the number of shafts (core area is expensive), then right-size the car and speed to the building height. For tall single-zone buildings the up-peak interval is necessarily longer — which is why real designs introduce zoning or sky-lobbies.

sim5.title: Sleep-Mode Payback
sim5.short: Compare always-on vs auto-standby; payback and savings.
sim5.insight: Enabling sleep mode cuts standby draw from {{before}} W to {{after}} W. Over {{idle}} idle hours a day that saves about {{kwh}} kWh and RM {{cost}} per year, avoiding {{co2}} kg CO₂. Because the change is usually a controller setting, payback is {{payback}}.
sim5.notes: Use with Module 4. Standby power runs 24/7, so even a small wattage adds up. Ask: a lift idle 20 h/day at 300 W wasted — how many kWh/year? (≈2,190.) Most modern controllers support sleep mode as a configuration, so the payback is often immediate.

sim6.title: VVVF vs Old-Drive
sim6.insight: Switching from {{from}} to {{to}} cuts annual traction energy by about {{pct}}% — roughly {{kwh}} kWh and RM {{cost}} per year, avoiding {{co2}} kg CO₂. The 1-speed drive draws a blunt rectangular pulse; the VVVF ramps power smoothly, so it wastes far less and gives a more comfortable ride.
sim6.notes: Use with Module 4/6. The load-vs-time chart is the teaching centrepiece: a 1-speed motor slams to full power (rectangular pulse), while VVVF ramps (trapezoid). Less peak, less heat, less wasted energy, smoother ride. Note that part of consumption is fixed (controls/aux) and isn't reduced by the drive upgrade.

sim7.title: Regenerative Drive
sim7.short: Visualise energy recovered when the motor generates.
sim7.insight: With a counterweight balancing the car plus {{balance}} of rated load, this lift regenerates on {{regenPct}} of the modelled trips. A regen drive recovers about {{recovered}} kWh/year, cutting net energy by {{reduction}}% — RM {{cost}} and {{co2}} kg CO₂ saved. Without it, that energy is burned as heat in a braking resistor.
sim7.notes: Use with Module 6. Key idea: a balanced lift spends roughly half its trips with the heavy side descending — that energy can be recovered instead of wasted as heat. Toggle grid feed-in off to show the savings vanish. Reductions of 20–35% match KONE/TKE/Mitsubishi case studies. Note: friction and inertia losses are never recoverable.

sim8.title: LED Retrofit Calculator
sim8.short: Cabin and shaft lighting savings and payback.
sim8.standard: Lighting energy; MyHIJAU grid CO₂ factor
sim8.insight: Replacing {{count}} × {{wBefore}} W {{type}} lamps with {{wAfter}} W LEDs cuts the cabin lighting load from {{loadBefore}} W to {{loadAfter}} W. Running {{hours}} h/day that saves {{kwh}} kWh and RM {{cost}} per year, avoids {{co2}} kg CO₂, and pays back in {{payback}}.
sim8.notes: Use with Module 4. Cabin lights often run 24/7. LED swaps are among the cheapest, fastest-payback energy measures and also cut heat load and maintenance (longer lamp life). Ask: if lamps run 24 h vs 12 h, how does payback change?

sim9.title: Escalator Operating Modes
sim9.short: Continuous vs auto-slowdown vs on-demand energy use.
sim9.insight: In {{mode}} mode this escalator uses about {{daily}} kWh/day ({{annual}} kWh/year). Versus running continuously that is a {{reduction}}% saving — RM {{cost}} and {{co2}} kg CO₂ a year. No-load power (turning empty) dominates, so slowing or stopping when no one is riding is where the savings come from.
sim9.notes: Use with Module 4/9. The big idea: an escalator turning empty still draws 30–55% of rated power. Auto-slowdown drops to a crawl when idle (~30–45% saving); on-demand stops entirely and restarts on a sensor (~50–70% saving). With peaky mall traffic there is lots of idle time to exploit. Ask: why is on-demand less suitable for very busy, continuous-flow escalators?

sim10.title: Fault Diagnosis Trainer
sim10.short: Branching decision trees for the top ten common faults.
sim10.question: Question
sim10.notes: Use with Module 3. Let trainees drive the tree and explain each choice. Every fault terminates within six questions. Emphasise the safety reminders — several faults (safety gear, brake, alarm) require taking the lift out of service immediately. Discuss when to stop and escalate rather than continue.

sim11.title: Maintenance Planner
sim11.short: Generate a statutory maintenance schedule and calendar.

gap.overdue: PMA inspection OVERDUE by {{days}} days — book DOSH/JKKP re-inspection now.
gap.dueSoon: PMA inspection due in {{days}} days — schedule the DOSH/JKKP inspection.
gap.ok: PMA inspection valid — next due in {{days}} days.

sim11.notes: Use with Module 5. The schedule is composed from a tagged task library filtered by lift type. The statutory PMA inspection (DOSH/JKKP) is annual — the gap analysis warns when it is due or overdue. Export to iCal to drop the plan into a facilities calendar. Older / heavier-used lifts get more recommended visits per year.

sim12.title: Hazard Hunt
sim12.short: Click-to-identify hazards in staged safety scenes.
sim12.instruction: Click each hazard you can spot.
sim12.notes: Use with Module 7 (safety). Let trainees click to find each hazard, then discuss the risk score (likelihood × severity) and the control hierarchy — engineering controls beat administrative beat PPE. Ask who is responsible for each fix. The scene report totals residual risk.

sim4.title: Energy Pie Calculator
sim4.short: Break a lift's annual energy into motor, standby, door and auxiliary.

results.classVsRange: This lift vs ISO classes A–G

sim4.insight: This lift uses about {{total}} kWh/year, costing roughly RM {{cost}} and emitting {{co2}} kg CO₂. {{driver}} dominates the energy use. Higher usage categories shift the balance toward the motor; long idle periods make standby power matter more — which is why auto-standby and efficient controllers pay off.
sim4.notes: Use this with Module 4 (Energy Performance). Ask trainees: for a lightly-used residential lift (category 1), what dominates — motor or standby? Common misconception: people assume the motor is always the biggest consumer. For low-traffic lifts, standby and lighting can exceed traction energy over a year. Try category 1 vs category 6 and watch the donut change.
